newsitem.title: FRANCE: France orders envoy to demand Kinshasa protection.
newsitem.headline: France orders envoy to demand Kinshasa protection.

text.p: France ordered its ambassador to Kinshasa on Wednesday to demand that self-proclaimed president Laurent Kabila protect French nationals and refugees after the killing of two French businessmen in the capital.

Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt told a briefing: "Our ambassador in Kinshasa is going to contact the new Congolese authorities at the highest level to transmit the following message: firstly to express our distress over the killing of our two compatriots and demand very firmly that measures be taken to ensure the French community's safety."

He said ambassador Michel Rougagnou was also instructed to express France's deep concern at the fate of refugees and displaced persons in the east of the country, renamed Democratic Republic of Congo from Zaire.
He would also demand that relief organisations and the United Nations be granted immediate access to the area.
"Thirdly, we want the new authorities to respect the rules of democracy and organise free elections, monitored by the international community, very rapidly," Rummelhardt said.

The spokesman said the French envoy was ordered to express Paris' concern for regional stability and urge strict respect of international borders, an apparent reference to fears that the conflict could spread into neighbouring Congo, Angola and the Central African Republic.

The two Frenchmen were shot dead on Tuesday night by men in uniform as they were leaving a factory in Kinshasa's Limete district, according to a French diplomat. The identity of the killers and their motives were not immediately clear.
An undercurrent of anti-French feeling surfaced in Kinshasa in the final days of President Mobutu Sese Seko's 32-year rule in the vast central African state he called Zaire.
Spokesmen for Kabila's rebel forces said before they took Kinshasa that hardline Mobutu loyalists might start killing foreigners to provoke intervention by their governments.

French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette and Justice Minister Jacques Toubon said in separate radio interviews they believed the shootings of the two Frenchmen were isolated incidents not meant as reprisals against France for its longtime support for Mobutu.
Toubon, asked if French citizens should now leave the country, told Europe 1 radio there was "no reason to panic".
Prime Minister Alain Juppe defended France's much-criticised stance on the conflict, telling reporters:

"It is to France's honour that it was one of the very few countries in the world to denounce from the outset the humanitarian disaster in eastern Zaire and to appeal to the international community -- alas, in vain -- to mobilise relief."
A multinational force was never put in place despite approval by the United Nations after most of the refugees fled Zaire to return to their homes in Rwanda and Burundi.

Juppe made no reference to France's longtime friendship with Mobutu, a 66-year-old autocrat who had ruled since 1965 but fled into exile after Kabila's forces swept across the country in just seven months.
